analysis.one_liner: Requires union representation elections to wait at least 35 days after workers file a petition.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee it was referred to, dying without a hearing or vote in the 113th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite National Labor Relations Board election rules. When workers petition for a union vote, the NLRB would have to wait at least 14 days before holding the pre-election hearing, and the election itself could not happen until at least 35 days after the petition is filed [S2]. The NLRB could not certify the results until it had ruled on every disputed issue, and employers would have to hand over a voter list with employees' chosen contact information [S2]. Introduced by Sen. Lamar Alexander in March 2014, it was a Republican response to the NLRB's rule shortening union election timelines; it was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never advanced [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially non-union companies facing an organizing drive, would gain at least 35 days to make their case to employees before any vote, plus time to litigate unit and eligibility disputes before results could be certified. The bill's supporters argue this gives both sides a fair chance to be heard and protects employees from voting before all the facts are on the table.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any election earlier than 35 calendar days after a petition is filed, and any pre-election hearing earlier than 14 days after filing, giving employers and employees alike more time before a vote.
Requires the NLRB to resolve every pre-election dispute and every challenge to the election's conduct or results before certifying who won.
Requires the employer to supply a voter list with each employee's name and one form of contact information the employee chooses, made available to all parties.

analysis.who_pays: Workers trying to form a union would wait longer to vote, and the extended period would fall during a campaign in which the employer controls the workplace and can hold mandatory meetings against the union. Unions would lose elections they might have won under a shorter timeline.

drawbacks.text: Mandating a minimum 35-day wait would make even uncontested elections slower than typical practice before the NLRB's rule — the delay applies in every case, not just complicated ones.

The waiting period falls while the employer controls the workplace and can require employees to attend anti-union meetings; longer campaigns have historically lowered the share of elections unions win.
Supporters of shorter elections argue that delays are exactly how organizing drives are worn down, and that workers who sign petitions want a vote promptly, not months later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aims — time for both sides to be heard, all disputes resolved before certification, accurate voter lists — are reasonable-sounding process goals. But its mechanism is a mandatory minimum delay in every election, which research and the NLRB's own rulemaking identified as favoring employers, who can use the extra weeks to campaign against the union in a workplace they control. For a worker who has already gathered majority support, the bill mainly adds weeks of exposure before a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Lamar Alexander introduced S. 2178 on March 27, 2014, joined by five original Senate cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the NLRB's shortened election timelines stayed in place and workers kept the ability to reach a union vote quickly; employers did not get the mandated waiting periods and slower certification they sought.

for.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
for.role: U.S. Senator from Tennessee; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to slow NLRB election timelines and referred it to the HELP Committee, where he was the senior Republican.

for.name: Business and employer associations
for.role: Industry groups opposing the NLRB's shortened election rule
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed legislation to lengthen union election timelines, framing the bill as due process for employers.

against.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Organized labor
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation lengthening union election timelines, arguing delays let employers campaign against organizing.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Republicans and the bill was a Republican response to the NLRB's election rule; the Democratic Senate majority never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would hand employers a guaranteed 35-day window, in a workplace they control, to campaign against a union before employees vote. Each additional week of delay has historically reduced the share of organizing elections workers win.

Slower elections and mandatory resolution of every dispute before certification would cut the number of successful organizing drives. Union success depends on momentum from the petition filing, which the bill's delays target.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and labor law firms
industries.note: Longer pre-election periods with extended hearings and more litigable issues create more billable work for firms that advise employers during organizing campaigns.
